lead: El Paso is a desert city, but it still floods. Monsoon storms off the Franklin Mountains, hard freezes and roof cooler leaks cause most of its water damage.
risk: monsoon flash floods, freeze damage and roof cooler leaks
why: El Paso sits on both sides of the Franklin Mountains, and rain that falls on the slopes rushes into arroyos and streets fast. In the summer of 2006, days of heavy monsoon rain flooded neighborhoods across the city. Water poured down from the mountains, filled streets and reached hundreds of homes. Summer storms still send water through low streets and yards, especially on the Westside and in the Northeast.

Cold is a surprise risk. In February 2011, a hard freeze dropped temperatures to near zero, rare for El Paso. Pipes burst across the city, and many homes had water pouring from walls and ceilings when the thaw came. Many El Paso homes also use evaporative coolers on the roof. A stuck float or cracked pan can leak into the attic and stain ceilings below.
image_caption: Hard freezes and roof cooler leaks surprise many El Paso homeowners.
problems: Westside and Northeast streets near arroyos
Attics and outside walls in hard freezes
Older homes in Five Points, Manhattan Heights
tips: Drain and cover an evaporative cooler each fall.
Insulate pipes in attics and outside walls.
Keep yard drains and street inlets clear before monsoon season.
Know if your home sits near an arroyo.
areas: Calls come from Kern Place, Sunset Heights, Manhattan Heights, Five Points, the Upper Valley, the Northeast, the Lower Valley and Eastridge, plus Socorro, Horizon City and Canutillo.

faq.q: Why is my El Paso ceiling leaking when it hasn't rained?
faq.a: A common cause is the evaporative cooler on the roof. If the float sticks or the pan cracks, water overflows into the attic and soaks the ceiling below. Turn off the cooler and its water line, then check the pan. DryFlare can dry the attic and ceiling.
